blocks.text: Executive definition of the game we are building

The project is publicly and officially presented as Symphony of Justice. Symphonia Iustitiae is preserved as the project's internal/original codename and may be referenced in internal documentation or historical materials.
The title represents one of the work's central foundations: a world built around different interpretations of justice and the conflicts that emerge among Judgment, Forgiveness, Vengeance, and Wisdom.
For international identity, investor materials, public communications, and commercial presentation, Symphony of Justice will be used as the primary title.

Symphony of Justice is planned as a story-driven real-time Action RPG with long-term character collection systems, centered on building and developing teams of characters with different professions, elements, abilities, talents, combat roles, and individual mechanics.

Combat is designed as a real-time third-person system in which player execution and strategic understanding work together. The player controls an active character directly, uses attacks and abilities with cooldowns and resources, reads enemy telegraphs, dodges and repositions, and can change between members of the party to combine their kits. Each character provides different offensive, defensive, support, elemental, or special possibilities, allowing strategy to emerge from individual identity and team synergy.

Outside combat, exploration is a major component of the project. The player can travel through different territories, complete missions, participate in special activities, obtain progression materials, uncover narrative information, and access new areas of the world.

The long-term product may include a Gacha-style character acquisition system, but the current gameplay identity is defined first by the quality of the RPG, its characters, exploration, combat, and worldbuilding.
The original vision for Symphony of Justice is multiplatform, with the long-term intention of reaching players on console, PC, and mobile devices.
Platforms considered for the complete product vision are:
Development will not target all platforms simultaneously.

The primary development and validation platform will be PC, where the first prototypes, playable demo, and Vertical Slice will be developed. Other platforms will be evaluated later according to the technical, financial, and commercial results of the early production stages.
The platform objectives are therefore separated as follows:
Future short-term multiplatform vision: mobile devices, subject to technical and market validation.
The project will be developed using Unreal Engine 5 as its primary engine.

This choice supports the intention to build a 3D game with combat, exploration, character systems, visual effects, animation, interfaces, and environments capable of scaling toward a larger production.
The technological architecture will be developed progressively and may combine:
Unreal Engine 5 as the primary engine.
C++ for systems requiring greater control, scalability, or performance.
Blueprints for prototyping, tools, and gameplay logic where appropriate.
Data-driven systems for characters, statistics, abilities, professions, elements, items, enemies, and progression.
Unreal Engine visual effects, animation, audio, and cinematic systems.
Version control for code, configuration, project assets, and production resources.
Automated build and development workflows where they provide clear production value.
Online infrastructure and backend services in later phases, when social or multiplayer systems require implementation.

Specific tools and versions may change during technical testing. Their exact versions should therefore be documented in the project's technical documentation rather than treated as permanent decisions at this stage.

Server deployment, future multiplayer architecture, data handling, privacy, regional security requirements, and legal permissions must be reviewed according to each target territory. Technologies such as Nakama, Epic Online Services, custom backend services, or dedicated servers may be evaluated when the project reaches the appropriate online-development milestone.
Symphony of Justice is currently in advanced pre-production.
The project has an extensive conceptual foundation developed over several years, including documentation related to:

The project is currently undergoing a consolidation and reorganization process. Historical documents are being used as source material to produce a new official, coherent, versioned documentation set.

This stage is intended to transform the existing concept work into concrete production specifications, define which systems remain part of the current vision, and prepare development of a functional prototype followed by a polished Unreal Engine 5 Vertical Slice and public-facing playable demo.
Explain the game in 1 to 3 sentences.
What is the main promise of the experience?

Symphony of Justice is a story-driven Action RPG set in a fantasy world divided by different interpretations of justice, where each nation, faction, and character defends ideals that can come into conflict even when all sides believe they are acting correctly.

The player explores this world, uncovers its secrets and conflicts, meets and develops characters with different elements, professions, talents, relationships, and combat identities, and builds teams to overcome enemies and challenges while progressing through a story that repeatedly questions what it actually means to act justly.

The central promise of Symphony of Justice is an experience in which strategy, characters, exploration, and narrative are connected. The player should not merely collect heroes and increase their power, but understand their ideals, contradictions, relationships, and consequences within a world where there is no single universal answer to what is right or wrong.

In Symphony of Justice, the player initially experiences the world from the perspective of a traveler and explorer who stands outside many of the political, historical, and cultural conflicts dividing the nations.

The journey begins with a personal need to understand events that the protagonist does not fully comprehend. Over time, that search draws the player into relationships, factions, and conflicts whose interpretations of justice may contradict one another.

The primary fantasy is not about turning the player into the center of the entire world. Instead, the goal is to make the player feel like someone entering a story far larger than themselves, able to travel through it, understand its competing perspectives, and gradually discover which events shaped the reality they now observe.

As the journey continues, the player stops being only an observer. The people encountered throughout the world begin to travel alongside the protagonist, allowing the player to build parties formed by individuals from different professions, elements, cultures, organizations, and ideologies.
The player therefore fulfills two fantasies simultaneously:
As the protagonist: a traveler seeking answers and gradually uncovering the truth behind the world.
As the player: the person who assembles, develops, and directs a group of characters whose abilities and relationships can be used to overcome the challenges of the journey.
What power, responsibility, or freedom does the player experience?

The player's greatest power is not simply increasing statistics or obtaining stronger characters. Their greatest capability is understanding the world and learning how to use the differences among its inhabitants.
Throughout the journey, the player progressively gains freedom to:
explore different territories and discover their histories;
meet characters from different nations and organizations;
build teams according to their preferred playstyle;
develop the capabilities, professions, elements, and talents of their characters;
experiment with different combinations and synergies;
approach situations through different tactical perspectives;
discover information that can change their perception of characters, conflicts, and earlier events.
The player's narrative responsibility is to search for answers without automatically assuming that a nation, character, or ideology represents absolute good or evil.

The world is built around different interpretations of Judgment, Forgiveness, Vengeance, and Wisdom. Progress therefore means learning the motives behind each group's decisions and confronting the consequences those decisions have created.

In gameplay terms, this freedom is represented through the ability to build and develop different character compositions, allowing the player to find their own solutions to challenges instead of depending permanently on a single required team.
What emotions do we want to create?
The experience of Symphony of Justice primarily aims to generate a combination of curiosity, discovery, attachment, uncertainty, tension, and strategic satisfaction.
The player should constantly feel that there is more behind what they are currently seeing.
Nations, characters, organizations, ruins, documents, Codex entries, and historical events should create questions and encourage the player to continue exploring in search of answers.
Exploring a new nation or meeting a new character should feel like entering a different part of a large world that existed long before the protagonist arrived.
The player does not only discover places. They discover cultures, conflicts, relationships, secrets, and different versions of the same history.
Doubt should be one of the central emotions.

The player may understand a character's reasons without agreeing with them, discover positive actions performed by questionable people, or encounter harmful consequences caused by people who genuinely believed they were acting correctly.

The intention is not to force the player into a constant binary choice between “good” and “evil,” but to encourage questions about what can be considered just depending on who experiences the consequences of a decision.
Characters should feel like individuals who belong to the world, not merely combat units obtained by the player.

Learning about their past, profession, relationships, ideals, contradictions, and evolution should allow the player to form bonds with them and provide narrative reasons, in addition to mechanical reasons, to use and develop them.
The story should maintain the feeling that every answer may create even larger questions.
Visions, secrets, conflicts among nations, and events tied to the past should build anticipation around what is truly happening and where the journey is leading.

When the player understands how their characters work and creates an effective composition, victory should feel like the result of understanding the systems rather than simply possessing superior statistics.
A successful encounter should be able to feel earned because the player correctly understood their team, the enemy, and the conditions of the fight.
The central fantasy of Symphony of Justice can be summarized as follows:

To be a traveler who enters a world divided by different ideas of justice, guided by visions that arrive through dreams; to gather people shaped by those same divisions; and, while learning to fight alongside them, to discover that understanding the truth may be far more difficult than defeating an enemy.

The design pillars of Symphony of Justice are principles that must remain present throughout the development of its systems, content, and overall player experience. They are not individual features. They are criteria used to determine whether a new mechanic, character, activity, or piece of content genuinely contributes to the project's identity.
For the current Game Vision, four primary pillars are defined.
Characters must differ not only through appearance, rarity, or statistics, but through the way their profession, element, talent, personality, and role in the world are translated into gameplay.
Each character should possess an identity clear enough for the player to understand what they contribute to the party and to find both mechanical and narrative reasons to use them.
relationships and possible synergies with other characters;
The goal is for acquiring a new character to mean more than obtaining higher numerical values. It should introduce a new possibility, interaction, or playstyle.
How does this appear in actual gameplay?
A character can change how the player builds a team through a mechanic that belongs specifically to them.

For example, a protection-focused character may react when an ally takes damage; a summoner may alter the number or type of entities present in combat; a medic may convert part of their healing into protection; or particular professions may receive benefits when interacting with specific elements.
Relationships between certain characters may also generate particular interactions, provided these interactions reinforce identity without turning one specific composition into a mandatory choice.
The player should gradually be able to recognize:
“This character plays this way because their playstyle represents who they are in the story.”
Decisions that do NOT fit this pillar
two characters fulfill essentially the same role and differ only in statistics or appearance;
rarity is the only reason a new character replaces an older one;
a character's personality or profession has no meaningful relationship with their gameplay identity;
a new character automatically invalidates older characters purely to increase commercial appeal;
every character can perform all functions without meaningful trade-offs or differences;
relationships between characters force the player to use unique mandatory compositions in order to remain competitive.
Pillar 2. Strategy through Synergy and Adaptation
Combat should primarily reward understanding characters, abilities, enemy behavior, and interactions among systems, rather than only accumulating statistics.
Team construction should represent a strategic decision.
Elements, professions, talents, roles, and abilities may interact to create different solutions to the same challenge.
Synergies should not be limited to increasing damage. They may also affect:
How does this appear in actual gameplay?
Before and during an encounter, the player analyzes enemy characteristics and decides which characters can function effectively together.

A strong composition should not necessarily be the one formed by the individually strongest characters. It should be a composition in which each character's combat style complements, enables, protects, or amplifies another character or the team as a whole.
Professions and elements can create particular compatibilities, while individual talents can introduce exceptions and strategies unique to each character.
Decisions that do NOT fit this pillar
increasing statistics is always better than understanding mechanics;
one optimal composition solves nearly all content;
elemental reactions are reduced to damage multipliers only;
new characters are designed primarily to replace older ones;
combat is consistently solved by repeating the same action sequence;
the player has no reason to adapt strategy to the enemy or environment;
an encounter requires a specific Gacha-acquired character in order to be completed.
Pillar 3. Explore to Discover and Progress
Exploration must serve both gameplay and narrative purposes.

Traveling through the world should not be limited to moving between primary objectives. Regions should allow the player to discover resources, stories, characters, activities, secrets, and elements that deepen their understanding of the nations and organizations that form the world.
Exploration is also one of the primary connections between combat and progression.

The player goes into the world to discover and obtain resources. Those resources help develop characters and prepare for new challenges. Those challenges then grant access to additional places, stories, and opportunities.
How does this appear in actual gameplay?
During exploration, the player may encounter:
information related to characters and past events.
Regions should differ in more than visual decoration. Their culture, inhabitants, activities, dangers, and systems should communicate what kind of society the player is traveling through.
Exploration should provide two rewards simultaneously:
Progression: the player obtains resources or access to new activities.
Knowledge: the player understands more about the world and what happened within it.
Decisions that do NOT fit this pillar
most of the territory lacks meaningful activity;
exploration consists only of following markers;
different nations are mechanically identical and only their decoration changes;
collectibles exist only to artificially increase playtime;
important materials require constant repetition of identical activities without meaningful variation;
the player is punished for exploring outside the expected route;
map size is prioritized over density and content quality.
Pillar 4. A World of Perspectives, Not Simple Answers
The narrative of Symphony of Justice must present a world where different cultures, characters, and organizations hold their own interpretations of Judgment, Forgiveness, Vengeance, and Wisdom.

The goal is not to claim that every perspective is equally correct. The intention is to allow the player to understand why those perspectives exist, what consequences they create, and what contradictions appear when different ideals attempt to coexist.
Characters must be part of these conflicts rather than existing separately from them.
Their history, profession, nation, relationships, and decisions should reveal different perspectives on the world.
How does this appear in actual gameplay?
The player may enter a region with an initial perception of an organization or character and later discover information that changes that interpretation.
The narrative should allow certain battles to carry weight because the player understands why the conflict exists, not simply because there is another enemy to defeat.
The progressive discovery of information should itself be part of the reward for advancing.
Decisions that do NOT fit this pillar
an entire nation is presented simply as good or evil;
conflicts have no visible consequences for the world or its inhabitants;
large amounts of lore replace the player's direct experience;
all important information is delivered through large blocks of text;
narrative context contradicts the player's gameplay actions without justification;
factions, characters, or conflicts are introduced only to artificially increase the size of the universe.
Role of the Gacha System in Relation to the Pillars
Although Symphony of Justice is envisioned as a long-term RPG that may use a Gacha-style character acquisition model, Gacha is not currently treated as an independent design pillar.

Gacha primarily represents a method of acquiring and distributing characters and content, while the pillars describe the experience those characters and that content must provide after they become part of the game.
Any future Gacha design must therefore respect the pillars above rather than weaken them.
In particular, the acquisition model should not cause:
characters to lose value too quickly;
strategy to depend primarily on spending;
specific content to become practically impossible without limited characters;
duplicate acquisition to be the only way to make a character functional;
monetization to take priority over coherent progression or player experience.
The specific rules of the Gacha system will be defined in its specialized design document.
What differentiates Symphony of Justice from other RPGs and character-collection games?
Which systems are distinctive to the project?
What can be communicated visually in a 30-second pitch?
The Unique Selling Points of Symphony of Justice represent the elements that can help the project build a recognizable identity within the character-driven RPG space.

These differentiators are still being consolidated. Some come directly from concepts developed in earlier versions of the project, while their final rules must later be validated in the specialized documents for combat, characters, progression, elements, and Gacha.
1. Characters Defined by Multiple Layers of Identity
One of the project's primary proposed differentiators is that a character is not defined only by rarity, element, or combat role.
A character's gameplay identity may be formed through the combination of:
history and function within the world.
The intention is for these layers to interact and create characters with different behaviors and strategic possibilities.

A profession represents what a character knows how to do within the world. Their element determines part of their combat interactions. Their personal talent introduces an individual characteristic that can alter the way their kit functions.
As a result, two characters who share the same element or broad combat role should not necessarily play in the same way.
Characters are designed from who they are within the world, and that identity is translated into gameplay rules.
This aims to connect narrative design and combat design rather than treating them as unrelated components.
2. Synergies Built through Elements, Professions, and Relationships
The team-building system aims to go beyond the traditional combination of damage, defense, and support roles.
Compositions may gain interactions through several dimensions:
May favor particular strategies or change how a resource or interaction is used.
May alter the behavior or value of an ability depending on the party around the character.
May create a specific interaction related to their relationship, history, or shared combat logic.
This allows the same unit to gain different value depending on the people used alongside them.

Relationships between characters are not intended to exist only as dialogue or optional narrative content. Some may become gameplay tools, provided they do not force the player into one mandatory composition.
Building a team means understanding how its members relate to one another mechanically and narratively, not simply adding their statistics together.
3. A Reaction System with Effects beyond Damage
Elements form another important layer of the strategic system.
Reactions are not intended to function only as offensive multipliers. Depending on the interaction, they may create effects such as:
temporary objects, zones, or effects in the combat space;

In addition to the standard elemental framework of the world, the project's conceptualization includes special powers such as Chaos, Illumination, Spectrum, Seals, and Time Clock, whose rules may differ from conventional elemental affinities.

These special powers can potentially interact with standard elements in distinctive ways. Historical concepts include, for example, Chaos reducing elemental resistances, Illumination empowering elemental effects, and Spectrum storing an element and later releasing it as an area effect.

These examples are design concepts rather than final balance commitments. The quantity, conditions, and final behavior of the reactions must be reviewed in the Elements and Reactions document and validated through prototyping.

The original project concept proposes that progression associated with acquiring additional copies of a character may be represented through a Legacy Card rather than only through an abstract numerical upgrade.
Each fragment of this progression may represent an event, memory, relationship, decision, or important moment from that character's life.

Visually, the Legacy Card is conceived as a stained-glass composition that is progressively completed. At the same time, each fragment can modify, expand, or reinterpret specific characteristics of the character's kit.

The system draws on the finite-copy progression structure used by other character-collection games, with a proposed endpoint reached after obtaining six additional copies beyond the original character unlock. The final quantity and commercial implementation remain subject to later review.

The stained glass is intended to depict the character's most essential self or the moment that defined their life. Each fragment has a title and meaning connected to the character, allowing players interested in story and theorycrafting to discover additional details or interpret the symbolism behind the complete image.
The purpose of this system is to connect mechanical progression with narrative meaning rather than treating duplicate acquisition as an entirely detached statistical layer.
5. Collecting Characters Means Discovering Perspectives on the World
The world of Symphony of Justice is constructed around different interpretations of Judgment, Forgiveness, Vengeance, and Wisdom.
Characters belong to these societies, organizations, and conflicts. Acquiring and learning about new characters therefore allows the player to observe the same world through different perspectives.
The intention is for character collection to serve more than a strategic purpose.
Each character may simultaneously function as:
a meaningful projection or emotional connection;
a connection to a nation, faction, or organization;
a different perspective on events in the world.
A new character should therefore provide both gameplay value and narrative value.

Symphony of Justice aims to differentiate itself through characters whose narrative identity has gameplay consequences, a team-building system based on professions, elements, talents, and relationships, and combat in which synergy can change the conditions of an encounter instead of only increasing statistics.

The goal is for the player to become interested in a character not only because that character is powerful, but because of who they are, what possibilities they introduce, and who they can meaningfully work with.
Similar types of experiences they are likely to enjoy.
Main motivations: story, collection, strategy, exploration, social interaction, and long-term progression.

The target audience of Symphony of Justice is primarily composed of players interested in character-driven RPG experiences, narrative, strategic team building, exploration, collection, and long-term progression.

The project's original documentation initially imagined a teenage and young-adult audience, approximately 15 to 21 years old, interested in both casual exploration and deeper team-building or competitive content.

At the current design stage, the recommendation is to broaden this definition and distinguish between a primary audience and several player profiles instead of restricting the product to a narrow age bracket.
Older teenagers and young adults, approximately 16 to 30 years old.
The project primarily seeks players who:
are interested in fantasy universes with substantial narrative depth and worldbuilding;
find satisfaction in experimenting with team compositions and strategies;
are familiar with or interested in games that receive periodic content updates;
can move between casual play sessions and activities requiring greater strategic depth.

The exact age rating and audience classification must be reviewed later according to the final narrative content, depiction of violence, commercial systems, regional regulations, and the applicable age-rating boards.
Rather than treating the audience as a single type of player, Symphony of Justice can support several motivations within the same experience.
This player is primarily interested in:
discovering the origins of nations and organizations;
understanding different perspectives on a conflict.
World missions, exploration, character stories, regional narratives, and events can serve as important content sources for this profile.
This player finds satisfaction in understanding systems and discovering efficient or creative combinations.
The objective is not merely to obtain powerful characters, but to learn how to use them together.
For this profile, an important part of the enjoyment comes from asking:
“What can I build with the characters I have?”
The profession system, elemental affinities, unique talents, and synergy concepts are particularly relevant to this type of player.
This player develops an especially strong relationship with the roster.
They may become interested in a character because of:
connection to a particular nation or faction.
Characters should have enough identity for different players to form personal preferences even when more efficient alternatives exist.
This profile especially enjoys seeing their account, roster, and builds develop over long periods of time.
Exploration, hunts, missions, guild-related activities, combat challenges, and progression systems can provide different paths for this type of player.
There should be a clear sense of growth, while avoiding progression that becomes only mandatory repetition of identical activities.
Experiences This Audience Is Likely to Enjoy
The original documentation does not establish specific existing games as official references.
For this reason, at the current stage it is more appropriate to define the categories of experiences that the target audience is likely to share.
Experiences in which each party member has a recognizable identity, personal history, and gameplay style.
Games in which team construction, timing, abilities, interactions, and synergies influence combat outcomes.
Games in which traveling through regions, finding secrets, completing missions, and discovering stories are part of the primary gameplay loop.
Experiences that receive new characters, events, stories, challenges, regions, or activities after launch.
Games with factions, cultures, historical events, relationships, and mysteries capable of encouraging investigation, discussion, speculation, and community theorycrafting.
Specific games used later as references or benchmarks should be defined in a dedicated Competitive Analysis, clearly separating inspiration, market comparison, and original design.
The audience motivations can currently be organized in the following order of importance:

Symphony of Justice is primarily aimed at older teenagers and young adults interested in character-driven RPGs, strategic team building, expansive narrative universes, and exploration. It is intended to support different levels of engagement, from players who mainly want to discover stories and characters to players who enjoy optimizing compositions and progressing over the long term.
Secondary audience: players outside this range who share the same motivations.
Primary profile: RPG player interested in characters, narrative, strategy, exploration, and long-term progression.
What should a player feel during the first hour?
What should they understand by the end of the demo?
What should they remember after closing the game?
The Experience Goals of Symphony of Justice define what the player should experience, understand, and remember during their first contact with the project.

These goals do not yet represent the final structure of the tutorial, prologue, or Vertical Slice. They serve as a guide for deciding which information, emotions, and systems should be prioritized when those experiences are designed.
1. What should a player feel during the first hour?
The first hour should primarily create a combination of:
curiosity, discovery, progressive familiarity with the systems, and the sense that something much larger exists beyond what the player is currently seeing.
The player should not receive a complete explanation of the world immediately. The experience should begin by showing only a small part of it and allowing questions to emerge naturally.
From the first minutes, there should be a personal question that motivates progress.

The protagonist's visions and connection to another person act as the first narrative thread. The player should understand that the journey begins with a personal motivation while gradually realizing that what the protagonist is searching for is connected to much larger events.
“I do not fully understand what is happening yet, but I want to find out.”
The Feeling of Entering a World That Already Existed
The player should not feel as though the world began when they arrived.
characters who already have relationships with one another;
locations with concrete social or historical functions;
events for which the protagonist does not yet have full context.
The objective is to communicate that Symphony of Justice has a past, a present, and consequences, and that the player begins their journey in the middle of that continuity.
The first hour should provide a small sample of the game's different forms of interaction without overwhelming the player.
at least one elemental or strategic interaction;
a reward that demonstrates some form of progression.
The purpose is not to teach every system.
The first hour should demonstrate the game's promise while reserving deeper systems for later moments.

The player should experience at least one situation where understanding an ability, element, profession, character mechanic, or interaction produces a result that is clearly better than simply attacking without thought.
The experience should establish early that:
Understanding the team will matter as much as increasing its statistics.
The first battle may be simple, but a later encounter should allow the player to discover a combination, reaction, or utility that creates a small moment of realization.
By the end of the first hour, the player should have met at least one or several characters who are memorable for more than their appearance.
The player should begin to remember them through elements such as:
function within the world or a hierarchy;
a relationship with the protagonist or another character.
This begins demonstrating one of the project's fundamental principles:
Characters are inhabitants of the world before they are combat units.
Before the end of the first experience, an event, conversation, environmental clue, or discovery should demonstrate that something which initially appeared simple has another interpretation.
This does not need to be a major plot twist.
It may be a political contradiction, new information about a faction, the true motivation of a character, or an unexpected consequence.
The objective is to introduce one of the central themes of the project from the beginning:
In Symphony of Justice, understanding who is right will not always be simple.
2. What should the player understand by the end of the demo?
The demo or Vertical Slice should function as a condensed representation of the product's identity.
By the end, the player does not need to know every mechanic or fully understand the lore.
They should, however, be able to clearly explain what kind of game they have just experienced and why it has a distinct identity.
They should understand the central fantasy
The player should understand that they are following a person who is gradually becoming involved in conflicts much larger than their original personal search.
They should perceive exploration and the discovery of information as fundamental parts of the experience.
They should understand how combat works
Without knowing every formula, the player should understand that encounters involve:
reading enemies and adapting to their behavior.
“I understand the basic rules, but I can see that there is much more depth to learn.”
They should understand why the characters matter
The player should clearly distinguish among the characters available during the demo.
a reason to belong in a particular composition.
We do not want the player to finish thinking:
“The blue one heals and the red one deals more damage.”
We want them to remember who those characters were and what made them different.
They should understand the connection between exploration and progression
The demo should demonstrate that exploration is not merely a transition between battles.
The player should see that traveling through the world can reveal:

The project's historical documents already describe exploration as a way to obtain ascension materials, enemy drops, and other resources necessary for developing characters. These ideas must be reviewed and adapted to the current progression system, but the core relationship between exploration and growth remains important.
They should understand the narrative identity
By the end of the demo, it should be clear that the world is built around different perspectives on concepts such as:
The player does not need to learn the full genealogy of the clans or the complete history of the deities.
They do need to understand that:
Different groups believe they are acting correctly, and those differences create the conflicts of the world.
They should understand that there is much more of the world to discover
The demo should close a small arc while leaving deliberate questions open.
an object or document the player cannot yet fully understand.
“The story I just played reached a conclusion, but I clearly saw only a small part of something much larger.”
3. What do we want the player to remember after closing the game?
The memories that remain after a player leaves an experience are especially important to the project's identity.
We do not want the primary impression to be simply:
Ideally, after several hours or even the following day, at least four memories should remain.
Something specific enough that the player can describe that character later.
This reinforces the idea that characters are one of the main gateways into the universe of Symphony of Justice.
The player should remember a situation in which a combination produced a special result.
apply an element -> switch to another character -> trigger a reaction -> change the conditions of the encounter.
Or use a character's unique mechanic to survive a situation that initially appeared lost.
The player should leave the experience with at least one question.
Not a question caused by poor explanation, but by intentional curiosity.
Why does the protagonist have those visions?
What really happened between the nations?
Why did a particular character act that way?
What does the legacy of the deities actually mean?
What exists behind the conflict the player has just witnessed?
A strong opening experience should end with one answer and two new questions.
The player should remember that Symphony of Justice is a world built around different interpretations of what can be considered just.
We do not want them to remember only beautiful cities or powerful characters.
We want them to be able to summarize the feeling of the universe with an idea close to:
“Everyone believes they have reasons for what they do, and understanding those reasons can be as important as confronting them.”
The first experience has fulfilled its purpose if, at the end, a player can answer positively to questions such as:
1. Do I understand what kind of game Symphony of Justice is?
2. Can I explain the basic rules of combat?
3. Do I remember at least one character?
4. Do I understand that composition and synergy matter?
5. Do I want to explore more of the world?
6. Do I have a story question I want answered?
7. Can I identify something that differentiates the game from other RPGs I know?
8. Am I interested in continuing to play?
These questions can later be converted into measurable criteria for Vertical Slice playtesting.

The long-term vision for Symphony of Justice is to evolve from an initial playable demonstration into a large-scale, story-driven Action RPG capable of expanding progressively through new regions, characters, stories, activities, systems, and, if commercially sustainable, long-term character-acquisition and live-content features.

The project's historical documentation has envisioned an experience capable of growing over several years through additional narrative content, exploration, recurring activities, social features, and new playable characters.
This vision represents the potential direction of the complete product. It is not the immediate production scope.
Development must proceed through verifiable stages, beginning with a prototype and a Vertical Slice that first prove the project's fundamental pillars.

Full multiplayer and social systems are outside the initial Vertical Slice because the project must first demonstrate the quality of its core RPG experience before assuming the cost and complexity of production-scale online infrastructure.

The grant-funded or investment-facing demo may establish technical foundations for future online services, such as backend architecture, source-control/build infrastructure, telemetry, crash reporting, account or player-data abstractions, or preliminary online-service prototyping, without promising production-ready multiplayer in the slice itself.

The current development objective of Symphony of Justice is to transform the project's extensive conceptual foundation into a first playable experience capable of proving that its fundamental systems can work together.
The initial prototype is not intended to represent the final artistic quality, content volume, or full commercial scope.
Its purpose is to answer a fundamental question:

Is the core gameplay of Symphony of Justice understandable, engaging, and strategically meaningful when characters, real-time combat, abilities, elements, synergies, and basic exploration function together inside an actual playable experience?

Completing this milestone will validate the systems required for the polished Vertical Slice and public/investment demo, which will present those validated systems at a quality level much closer to the intended product.

The Core Gameplay Prototype must produce a playable PC build developed in Unreal Engine 5 that allows the player to complete a small gameplay cycle using functional, even if still provisional, versions of the fundamental systems.
The prototype should allow the player to:

Explore -> Find a challenge -> Enter combat -> Use different characters -> Combine abilities and elements -> Defeat the enemy -> Receive a reward -> Apply a basic improvement -> Continue the experience

4. Criteria for Declaring the Milestone Complete
The Core Gameplay Prototype can be considered complete only when it meets a verifiable Definition of Done.
The player can start and finish the experience without using Unreal Editor.
Real-time combat functions correctly at the prototype level.
The player can control characters and perform distinct actions.
Enemies can perceive, attack, react, and be defeated.
Functional victory and defeat conditions exist.
At least one elemental reaction can be completed.
At least one synergy between characters can be activated.
Exploration and combat coexist within the same playable flow.
The player receives a reward after completing an encounter.
No critical errors prevent the experience from being completed.
An external player should be able to understand:
why a particular composition may be useful;
how to respond to enemy behavior;
what they receive as a reward.
players can complete the primary gameplay loop;
necessary information can be interpreted through the interface and world feedback;
players can identify tactical problems or opportunities without depending constantly on external instructions.
The purpose of these tests is not to obtain artificially high satisfaction scores.
Their purpose is to identify what works and what must change before the project invests in higher-cost art and production.
